questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had heard that the study environment in Almería was great, and generally speaking, Spanish people are kind. Also, Almería is the sunniest city in Andalucía, however, that was not the case upon arrival (but the locals said it was odd too that the weather had changed so drastically)

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I've had a good experience studying abroad. The teachers usually have been helpful and understanding towards the Erasmus students - some more than others. It has been quite difficult interacting with the local students as many of them did not seem to want to engage with the foreign students - many Erasmus students held on tightly to one another. I was fortunate to meet locals outside of the university, which was a great advantage regarding further developing language skills.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: You had to look a bit for it, but the personnel of the host university were quite helpful in that matter. The volunteers of the ESN office has also been very helpful, and there has been a couple of WhatsApp groups where people can ask questions about everything.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: As previously stated, the personnel of the host university were helpful. I had to change some courses, and one of the ladies at the office was really helpful and provided a step-by-step guideline for me to follow as I was going to change my courses.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I did not have any issues with the orientation nor the assistance at the host institution.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I looked on AirBnB, which I believe was the easiest and cheapest option. I know from other sources that some people have been scammed by locals when looking for housing. A recommendation here is to bring along a mentor if you sign up for one - they are there to help you with questions of all sorts.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: A recommendation here is to bring along a mentor if you sign up for one - they are there to help you with questions of all sorts. Also, they help you so you do not get scammed by someone.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I lived in an AirBnB, which was great - and had circulating roommates, both English-speakers and Spanish natives. You will be able to find both as well at the dorm, Civitas, as well.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As I had done all of the work prior to arriving, I had no issues whatsoever in registering myself at the office at the registration day. The one doing the enrollment process was quite surprised as well.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I got to the office and had to draw a number in order to enter the office (you also booked your appointment online prior to arriving at the university). I entered the office when it was my turn, and the person responsible for my registration asked me whether I wanted to it in English or Spanish. As I had done all the work prior to arriving, the process only lasted 5 minutes. He gave me some information about the university, the campus site, where to find a doctor and so on.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The person responsible gave me a map of the campus site and numbers and names of the hospitals and doctors of Almería in case I needed it.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful in registering for the classes I wanted - HOWEVER, what the university fails to tell the incoming students is that a lot of the courses overlap (it is quite a common problem, and one of the issues they fix the most). So, in order to avoid that you need to look CAREFUL on the horario provided on their website - there are both theoretical and practical lessons, and these tend to overlap but usually that is NOT a problem (ask the professor of course - most of them knows that it is a recurrent problem)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Please fill out all of the information prior to arriving, it will make the process a whole lot easier AND less stressful.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some of the classes had a quite low level compared to that of Danish universities. I would say some of the courses could compare to the level of Danish high schools.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In Spain, you do not read as much as you do in Denmark - typically, you would just take notes from what the teacher is saying. Sometimes, there are a few exercises - but that is rarely the case. It seems more indoctrinating than in Denmark as the teacher speaks and the students take notes in the way that it is often not that interactive.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1) Latin American Literature II
2) Business communication in a foreign language: English
3) History and culture of Hispanic countries
4) Critical analysis of discourse in Spanish
5) Specialized use of Spanish

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I can highly recommend the course: Latin American Literature. The professor is absolutely amazing, and really takes the Erasmus students into account as the local students at times speak a little too fast and too low to hear - also, took great pride into knowing where everyone was from (we also had a poetry event in different languages). 
Also, the Critical analysis course has been great as well - the professors teaching the courses have been really welcoming and friendly.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not encounter any unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The food in Andalucía typically is a bit less expensive than that of the capital, Madrid. Also, in generally, housing and such is cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did enroll for the university gym, however the time set for a session (80 minutes or so) was way to short a period of time.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There has been plenty of clubs to attend (I did not) - these were also shown at the introduction day.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you want to broaden your network, while studying abroad, go on the trips that the ESN office provides. It makes your stay less lonely, and you'll make new friends, or acquaintances, that way.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to the nearby cities on the weekends; Granada, Córdoba, Cádiz, Sevilla. There is PLENTY to see. Also, in the region of Almería itself. 
Semana Santa (Easter) was a real treat to experience in Almería as it is something that the locals prepare for almost a year. It is worth staying in town during that period.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I would say it was quite easy, also given that I befriended Spanish people as well. Although, the siesta is still not my thing.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Instead of sitting with all of the Erasmus students all the time, try to sit close to the local students. Also, attend the events they go to at uni (in my case: poetry event) - it helped me speaking more with some of my fellow students. Importantly, a simple 'buenos días' or 'hola' in the morning or just in general when someone enters the classroom goes a long way.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did find the siesta really challenging, also that the local kiosks are closed during those hours. Furthermore, that Sunday indeed is a holy day in Spain - shops and everything alike are closed, bear that in mind.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I love that they are really welcoming and always say 'hi' or 'goodbye', or in the Almerian case 'hasta luego'/'see you later' although you might not see them later or ever again for that matter.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Get yourself involved with other Erasmus students (but bear in mind many do not speak Spanish)
2) Go on the trips, which are organized by the ESN office, or by the Sports Department
3) Have fun while studying there - it is not supposed to kill your joy for studying

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It will be difficult in the beginning - adjusting to the language, the surroundings, and the people. But it'll be all worth it in the end.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I guess that would be my Literature teacher - she was really the main reason that I had a great stay at UAL. She truly made a difference for me - I always looked forward to her classes.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge must have been when I wanted to change my courses as they overlapped. That was chaotic, but it all turned out well in the end.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I do not recommend anyone to take the course 'Usos Especializados del Español' - this course was truly confusing and not very intellectually simulating. The local students did not understand the concept or idea of the course very well either. Also, the teacher was nice, however, she did not take Erasmus students into account so it was difficult to attend her classes.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
